formal_diagnoses.value: CONTESTED between examining clinicians. Dr John G. Watkins, called by the defence, examined him under hypnosis and diagnosed multiple personality; a plea of not guilty by reason of insanity was entered one week later. Dr Martin T. Orne, called by the prosecution, examined him personally and concluded the contrary: 'It is concluded that Mr. Bianchi was simulating a multiple personality and the diagnosis of Antisocial Personality Disorder with Sexual Sadism was made.' Dr Donald T. Lunde, also for the defence but without hypnosis, reported to defence counsel that he was a 'pathological liar'. Dr Ralph B. Allison examined him as amicus curiae. Dr Ronald Markman consulted for the Los Angeles Public Defender's Office and his diagnosis remained privileged. Drs Charles M. Moffett and Saul J. Faerstein also examined him.

formal_diagnoses.notes: ONLY THE SECOND RECORD IN THE DATASET WITH THIS FIELD POPULATED, after USA-005-GACY, and the first where the disagreement is documented in peer-reviewed literature by the examining clinicians themselves, on both sides. That is why it is recorded despite being contested: the schema requires a diagnosis attributable to a named clinician who examined the subject, in a citable document, and here there are several, publishing against each other. The field records the disagreement; it does not resolve it. Note the asymmetry in what has been read: the Orne paper was retrieved and its abstract read verbatim; the Watkins paper was not. A contributor should read Watkins before this field is considered settled.

motive_classification.notes: Deliberately null, and the reason is worth stating because a tempting shortcut exists. Orne et al. recorded a diagnosis of Antisocial Personality Disorder with Sexual Sadism. A diagnosis is not a motive coding: one is a clinical classification of a person, the other a typological classification of offences, and the two are not interchangeable. The diagnosis is also contested by the examining clinician on the other side. Coding a Holmes & Holmes category from a contested diagnostic label would be two inferential steps away from the evidence, and this field takes none.

method_now_disputed.notes: Recorded with a caveat: his CONVICTION rested on a guilty plea, not on hypnotic evidence, so this is not a case of a conviction resting on a discredited technique. The field is populated anyway because the case is one of the reference points in the forensic-hypnosis literature, and a reader looking for discredited-method cases should find it here. confession_reliability.value: Very low, and found so by both a court and the prosecution's clinical examiner. His pre-trial testimony 'varied so much' that the Los Angeles County District Attorney moved to drop the charges against his co-defendant. The trial judge refused, holding there was enough evidence, and the state Attorney General's Office took over the prosecution. Under California law the co-defendant could not be convicted on accomplice testimony alone, so the case was carried by physical evidence. Orne et al. recorded 'a persistent pattern of conning and deliberate deception' and documented fabricated alibis, including one his own attorney recognised as false and the named woman later admitted was untrue. A defence examiner described him as a pathological liar.

confession_reliability.notes: This is the dataset's strongest documented case of an unreliable accomplice witness, and it is instructive precisely because the system handled it correctly. Compare USA-015-NORRIS, whose account was corroborated by physical recoveries he led police to; compare USA-003-HALL, where a confession produced nothing and the conviction rested on it anyway. Here the testimony was openly treated as near-worthless, the statutory corroboration rule did its work, and the co-defendant was convicted on fibre evidence and 250 witnesses instead. Note the structural point about plea bargains: the same agreement that secured his testimony is what makes the testimony weak, and in this case the incentive was the death penalty.
